text: A Scripted REST API gets consumed by systems outside the team's own control. The moment an external integration calls it, changing that Resource's request or response shape becomes risky — renaming a response property or adding a required field can silently break every caller still using the old shape, with no warning until something fails downstream.

A developer still needs to evolve the API over time without forcing every existing caller to change on the developer's schedule. That's what versioning is for. Each Scripted REST API can have multiple Version records attached to it, and every Version contributes its own base-path segment — v1 served at one URL, v2 served at another, both live at the same time.

Say v1's GET resource returns an equipment item's own fields. A new consumer needs its current checkout status too. Adding that directly to v1 would change what every existing caller receives, even ones who never asked for it. Instead, that change belongs in a brand new Resource script, under a new Version — v1's script stays exactly as it was, untouched.

That separation is deliberate. v2 is not v1's script with an if branch bolted on; it's its own Resource record with its own script. Because v1's script never changes, v1's behavior never changes either, no matter what gets added in v2.

That's the real payoff. An integration still calling the v1 URL keeps receiving exactly the shape it was built against, forever. The team ships v2 the moment it's ready, a new consumer starts using it immediately, and the old integration migrates to v2 on its own schedule, or never, if it doesn't need the new field at all.

No team has to coordinate a simultaneous cutover across every calling system — that's the real cost versioning avoids. Next, the lab: a versioned GET resource for the equipment-checkout app, built and explained end to end, with a v2 note on what could be added later without breaking v1.
